Bread of Adversity
BRED uv ad-VUR-si-tee
n. phr. (the straitened portion the Lord gives, named with the water of affliction)
Hebrew lechem tsar — lechem, bread; tsar, straitness, narrowness, distress; the pair with mayim lachats, water of oppression, is the prisoner's ration, the scant fare of a man under pressure.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

“And though the Lord give you the bread of adversity, and the water of affliction, yet shall not thy teachers be removed into a corner any more, but thine eyes shall see thy teachers: And thine ears shall hear a word behind thee, saying, This is the way, walk ye in it.” The phrase is the prisoner's ration — scant bread and short water, the fare Ahab ordered for Micaiah — and the first thing to mark is who serves it. Though the Lord give you: adversity here is not an accident befalling the people but a portion handed to them by God. The second thing is what is promised in the same breath. The affliction is not removed, and no relief is offered; instead the teachers are restored to sight and a voice is given behind them directing their steps. God's answer to the hard portion is His word and His instruction, which is exactly the answer the New Testament gives when it says that chastening is the Father's dealing with sons and yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness. The verse before it says the LORD waits to be gracious and that blessed are all they that wait for him; the verse after describes idols cast away. A straitened believer with his teachers before him and a word behind him has what Isaiah calls blessedness, though his bread is short.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Adversity, an event or series of events which oppose success or desire; misfortune; affliction. Bread, food in general; sustenance. The bread of adversity, Isaiah 30:20, the scant portion the Lord Himself gives, answered by teachers restored and a word behind.

expand to see more

Adversity, an event or series of events opposing success; affliction; distress.

Bread, food made of grain; in Scripture, sustenance or daily portion.

Hebrew tsar, straitness, narrowness, distress — hence scant bread.

Hebrew lachats, oppression or pressure; the water of affliction beside it.

Compare the prison ration ordered for Micaiah, 1 Kings 22:27.

Key Scripture

Isa 30:20 — "And though the Lord give you the bread of adversity, and the water of affliction, yet shall not thy teachers be removed into a corner any more, but thine eyes shall see thy teachers:"

Isa 30:21 — "And thine ears shall hear a word behind thee, saying, This is the way, walk ye in it, when ye turn to the right hand, and when ye turn to the left."

Isa 30:18 — "And therefore will the LORD wait, that he may be gracious unto you, and therefore will he be exalted, that he may have mercy upon you: for the LORD is a God of judgment: blessed are all they that wait for him."

Heb 12:11 — "Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby."

Modern Corruption

Adversity is reassigned to chance, to the devil, or to the sufferer's own failure of faith, and the verse's plain subject — the Lord who gives it — is removed.

expand to see more

The prosperity teaching cannot say this verse. On that scheme hardship is always the enemy's work or the believer's unbelief, never a portion served by God; and so a Christian in a long trouble is told to rebuke what Isaiah says the Lord has handed him. Scripture's own range is wider and more comfortable: the LORD kills and makes alive, forms the light and creates darkness, and does not afflict willingly but does afflict. Job received evil as well as good from the same hand and sinned not with his lips. Naming God as the giver of the hard portion is what makes patience possible, for a portion from a Father can be borne where a random misfortune cannot.

The opposite error is fatalism, which hears the giving and stops, leaving a believer resigned under a hand he does not love. The verse itself refuses that: the sentence does not end with the bread, it ends with the teachers in sight and a word behind the ear saying, This is the way, walk ye in it. The principle to recover is the Reformed doctrine of chastening. Affliction is fatherly, measured, and purposeful; God's customary provision in it is not escape but instruction, so the straitened Christian is to look for his teachers and listen for the word rather than wait for the bread to improve.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew lechem tsar, bread of straitness; mayim lachats, water of oppression — the prisoner's ration, given by the Lord and answered with teachers and a guiding word.

expand to see more

Hebrew lechem, bread or food, the daily portion of a household.

Hebrew tsar, straitness or distress; hence a scant and narrow ration.

Hebrew lachats, oppression or pressure, of the water of affliction.

Hebrew moreh, teacher — restored to sight in the same verse.

Followed by a word behind the ear: This is the way, Isaiah 30:21.

Usage

"though the Lord give you the bread of adversity, and the water of affliction"

"yet shall not thy teachers be removed into a corner any more"

"This is the way, walk ye in it"
